title: Speeding up Gravitational Lens Mass Models with Machine Learning: Applications in X-ray Astronomy
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS on 21 July 2026. 16 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. The full code pipeline to reproduce the simulations, neural network training and parameter predictions, along with the trained network models and optimisation code, are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/aostridge/Grav-Lens-ML. Comments are welcome!
summary: Multi-wavelength observations of quadruply lensed quasars constitute a powerful probe of cosmology, dark matter substructure along the line of sight, and the structure of X-ray emitting regions in high-redshift quasars. These investigations are conditional on acquiring an accurate model for the surface mass density of matter lensing these quasars. We propose a simulation-based machine learning method to accelerate parameter inference in real quadruply lensed systems by several orders of magnitude. We simulate a grid of quadruply lensed sources with Singular Isothermal Ellipsoid (SIE) lenses and use the projected positions of the four lensed images to train two fully connected neural networks that predict the mass parameter and ellipticity. For a large fraction of simulated systems, the neural network-initialised mass models converge in time-scales of a few minutes and recover the source position at the <0.''005 level for a broad range of lens masses and ellipticities. We apply our neural networks to seven quadruply lensed quasars, lensed by isolated galaxies or a galaxy-perturber pair, which have archival Chandra observations. The final optimised mass models for each quasar predict the observed lensed image positions in Gaia Data Release 3. These mass models enable the caustic method, which locates the X-ray-to-optical emission regions to milliarcsecond precision in these otherwise unresolvable systems, improving the effective angular resolution of Chandra at high-z by up to two orders of magnitude. Our approach accelerates this mass modelling by supplying informed initial parameters, enabling application to the many new quadruply lensed systems expected from forthcoming surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a simulation-based machine learning method using neural networks to rapidly predict mass parameters and ellipticities of quadruply lensed quasars, accelerating mass modeling from hours to minutes and enabling milliarcsecond-precision X-ray-to-optical emission region localization.
AI.motivation: Accurate mass modeling of quadruply lensed quasars is essential for cosmology, dark matter substructure studies, and quasar emission region analysis, but traditional parameter inference is computationally expensive and slow.
AI.method: Train two fully connected neural networks on simulated SIE lens grids using projected image positions to predict mass parameters and ellipticity, then apply to seven real quadruply lensed quasars with Chandra observations.
AI.result: Neural network-initialized models converge in minutes, recover source positions at <0.005 arcsecond level, and enable the caustic method to achieve milliarcsecond precision—improving Chandra's effective angular resolution at high-z by up to two orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: This ML acceleration makes mass modeling tractable for the large number of new quadruply lensed systems expected from forthcoming surveys, enabling detailed multi-wavelength studies of lensed quasars.

title: Charting the Galactic Underworld I: Comprehensive simulations of the kinematics, rates, and demographics of Milky Way black holes
comment: Submitted to AAS journals. Main text is 22 pages, 13 figures, and 3 tables. Interactive figures are available at https://www.tomwagg.com/html/interact/galactic-underworld.html
summary: With upcoming data from Roman, Gaia DR4, and spectroscopic surveys, we will soon have an unprecedented dataset of Milky Way black holes (BHs) to constrain their formation and evolution. To prepare, we simulate the intrinsic population of Milky Way BHs with cogsworth, self-consistently accounting for their binary evolution and trajectories through the Galactic potential. We report the rate, demographics, and kinematics of these BHs, and their sensitivity to 32 variations in binary evolution, supernova physics, and Galactic potentials. In the fiducial model, ~$1.7 \times 10^8$ BHs have formed in the Milky Way (though this total spans an order of magnitude across our variations), where the vast majority (~91%) are currently isolated and ~3% have escaped the Galaxy. Most of the ~$10^7$ BHs in binaries have another BH or a white dwarf companion, but ~$10^5$ retain a luminous stellar companion. BHs are distributed more diffusely than visible stars, with a scale height around ~$2.5\times$ larger. BH masses correlate with present-day location: the most massive BHs are preferentially close to the Galactic plane. This correlation is especially strong for BH-star binaries, which separate into tight, low-mass post-common-envelope systems and wide, high-mass non-interacting ones. The BH mass distribution and kinematics are highly sensitive to the remnant mass prescription and natal kick model, so observations could constrain explodability criteria and BH kicks. Accounting for the time-evolution of the Galactic potential more than doubles the escape fraction and increases the bound population's scale height by ~20%, whilst neglecting binary interactions overestimates it by 30%.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the cogsworth simulation framework to model the intrinsic population of Milky Way black holes (BHs), predicting ~1.7×10^8 BHs formed (spanning an order of magnitude across 32 model variations), with ~91% isolated, ~3% escaped, and most of the ~10^7 binary BHs paired with other BHs or white dwarfs. BH masses correlate with location (massive BHs near the plane), and the mass distribution/kinematics are highly sensitive to remnant mass and natal kick prescriptions, with binary interactions and time-evolving Galactic potential significantly affecting escape fractions and scale heights.
AI.motivation: To prepare for upcoming observational datasets (Roman, Gaia DR4, spectroscopic surveys) by simulating the Milky Way BH population to constrain BH formation and evolution.
AI.method: Simulated the intrinsic population of Milky Way BHs using cogsworth, self-consistently accounting for binary evolution and trajectories through the Galactic potential, exploring 32 variations in binary evolution, supernova physics, and Galactic potentials.
AI.result: ~1.7×10^8 BHs formed in the fiducial model (order-of-magnitude variation across models); ~91% isolated, ~3% escaped; ~10^7 BHs in binaries mostly with BHs or white dwarfs, ~10^5 with luminous companions; BH scale height ~2.5× larger than visible stars; BH masses correlate with Galactic plane proximity; mass distribution and kinematics highly sensitive to remnant mass and natal kick prescriptions.
AI.conclusion: Time-evolving Galactic potential more than doubles escape fraction and increases bound population scale height by ~20%, while neglecting binary interactions overestimates scale height by 30%. Observations can constrain explodability criteria and BH kicks via the BH mass distribution and kinematics.

title: Reionization driven by the few: the ionizing budget of galaxies at z=5-10 from JWST/NIRSpec
summary: The sources responsible for the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), the last major phase transition of the Universe, remain highly elusive. While JWST has begun to illuminate the properties of early galaxies, the direct detection of their ionizing photons is virtually impossible due to the neutral intergalactic medium (IGM) at z>6. A direct estimate of the escape fraction of ionizing photons (fesc) is thus not possible. However, the escape fraction is encoded in spectral features that trace a low opacity to ionizing photons, namely the reduction of nebular emission with increasing fesc. Here, we exploit the large archive of JWST/NIRSpec spectra at 5<z<10 from the DAWN JWST Archive to provide new constraints on the ionizing emissivity of EoR galaxies and on the timeline of reionization. Through detailed spectral fitting of 1428 galaxies with a picket-fence model for the escape of ionizing photons, we derive posteriors of fesc together with the effective ionizing output. This approach yields the escaping ionizing output of each galaxy while bypassing the usual decomposition into the ionizing photon production efficiency and fesc. Combining these measurements with UV luminosity functions (LFs), we derive the hydrogen ionizing LFs, resulting in an observationally-derived ionizing photon budget at 5<z<15, integrated down to MUV=-13. Under standard assumptions, our budget yields an evolution of the IGM neutral fraction consistent with independent probes, with reionization ending at z~5.8. Given the evolving shape of the ionizing LF, bright sources (MUV ~ -20) dominate the cosmic ionizing emissivity nion at lower redshift (z=5-6), whereas at z>6 faint galaxies (MUV > -18) contribute roughly equally. Remarkably, a mere ~20% of sources, those with fesc>10%, produce ~87% of the ionizing photons. Overall, our results support a picture in which a few strongly leaking galaxies drive most of reionization.

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRSpec spectra of 1,428 galaxies at z=5-10, the authors derive escape fractions of ionizing photons (fesc) and construct ionizing luminosity functions. They find that reionization ends at z~5.8, faint and bright galaxies contribute comparably at z>6, and only ~20% of sources (with fesc>10%) produce ~87% of ionizing photons, suggesting reionization is driven by a few strongly leaking galaxies.
AI.motivation: Direct detection of ionizing photons from EoR galaxies is impossible due to neutral IGM at z>6. The authors aim to constrain the ionizing emissivity of EoR galaxies and the reionization timeline by inferring escape fractions from spectral features in JWST/NIRSpec data.
AI.method: analyzed 1,428 galaxies at 5<z<10 from the DAWN JWST Archive using JWST/NIRSpec spectra; applied a picket-fence model for ionizing photon escape to derive fesc posteriors via detailed spectral fitting; combined measurements with UV luminosity functions to construct hydrogen ionizing LFs and compute the ionizing photon budget down to MUV=-13.
AI.result: Reionization ends at z~5.8; bright sources (MUV~-20) dominate at z=5-6 while faint galaxies (MUV>-18) contribute ~equally at z>6; only ~20% of sources with fesc>10% produce ~87% of ionizing photons.
AI.conclusion: A few strongly leaking galaxies (fesc>10%) drive most of reionization, consistent with independent probes of the IGM neutral fraction evolution.

title: Unsupervised selection and characterisation of Little Red Dots in JWST surveys with manifold learning
summary: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are compact, red sources discovered at high redshift by JWST whose physical nature and selection function remain debated. We investigate whether an unsupervised machine-learning approach applied to multi-band photometry can identify LRD-like objects, and other populations, without relying on predefined colour cuts. Using UMAP, a manifold-learning (dimensionality-reduction) method, we place ~242,000 isolated, well-measured sources from the ASTRODEEP-JWST catalogue on a two-dimensional map, where objects with similar broadband colours, morphology, and photometric redshift lie close together. We then use spectroscopically confirmed LRDs to identify where LRD-like objects lie within this map, compare the resulting areas with published colour cuts, and validate our data-driven selection against archival NIRSpec spectra from the DJA. We find that the spectroscopically selected LRDs concentrate in two well-defined regions with no colour cut imposed, tracing populations that differ mainly in redshift, a difference imprinted in their broadband colours. The main region reaches a purity of ~0.78 at ~0.82 completeness on the spectroscopically classified subset, competitive with, or cleaner than, literature colour cuts, and yields ~100 additional candidates. We also test the method as a general tool for population discovery: the manifold recovers the locations of brown dwarfs and broad-line AGN with no explicit criterion, and isolates rare pathological outliers. Overall, unsupervised manifolds, anchored by sparse high-confidence spectroscopic labels, provide an efficient, assumption-light framework for characterising populations, comparing selection methods on a common basis, and discovering rare objects in large photometric datasets.

AI.tldr: Using UMAP (unsupervised manifold learning) on ~242,000 JWST photometric sources, the paper identifies two distinct, compact regions corresponding to Little Red Dots (LRDs) without predefined colour cuts, achieving ~0.78 purity and ~0.82 completeness, and demonstrates the method's general utility for discovering populations like brown dwarfs, broad-line AGN, and rare outliers.
AI.motivation: The physical nature and selection function of Little Red Dots (LRDs) — compact, red high-redshift JWST sources — remain debated, and existing colour-cut-based selections may be biased or incomplete.
AI.method: Applied UMAP (unsupervised manifold learning/dimensionality reduction) to multi-band photometry of ~242,000 isolated, well-measured sources from the ASTRODEEP-JWST catalogue, placing objects on a 2D map based on broadband colours, morphology, and photometric redshift. Spectroscopically confirmed LRDs were used to identify LRD regions on the map, and results were validated against NIRSpec spectra from the DJA.
AI.result: Two well-defined LRD regions were identified without colour cuts, differing mainly in redshift. The main region achieves ~0.78 purity at ~0.82 completeness on spectroscopically classified data, competitive with literature colour cuts, and yields ~100 additional candidates. The manifold also recovers brown dwarfs, broad-line AGN, and rare outliers.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised manifold learning anchored by sparse high-confidence spectroscopic labels provides an efficient, assumption-light framework for characterising populations, comparing selection methods, and discovering rare objects in large photometric datasets.

title: Probing Dark Matter Substructure with Wave-Optics Distortions of Strongly Lensed LISA Gravitational Waves
summary: Strong lensing changes the phase of a gravitational-wave signal as well as its amplitude and arrival time. We study whether this phase information can distinguish three dark-matter structures in the lens: a Navarro--Frenk--White halo (NFW), a self-interacting halo (SIDM), and a fuzzy-dark-matter field (FDM). We generate waveforms for the detectable lensed massive-black-hole-binary population of a four-year LISA mission and fit every signal with the same smooth singular-isothermal-ellipsoid lens with external shear. In 132 lens systems, 311 images are resolved as separate signals in time. NFW and SIDM produce real waveform changes, but their slowly varying part is largely degenerate with the constant, gradient, and curvature of a smooth lens. The coherent density fluctuations of FDM leave a larger frequency-dependent residual after this fit. The NFW--FDM and SIDM--FDM populations become distinguishable with about 60 and 110 resolved image waveforms, respectively. These results show that repeated lensed LISA signals can probe the spatial form of dark matter in lens galaxies, rather than only the total lensing mass.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether strong lensing of gravitational waves from massive black hole binaries, as detectable by LISA, can distinguish between three dark matter models (NFW, SIDM, and FDM) by analyzing phase changes in lensed waveforms, finding that FDM is distinguishable from NFW and SIDM with ~60-110 resolved images due to its coherent density fluctuations leaving frequency-dependent residuals.
AI.motivation: To determine if phase information from strongly lensed gravitational-wave signals can differentiate between three dark matter halo models (NFW, SIDM, FDM) in the lensing galaxy, moving beyond total mass constraints to probing the spatial form of dark matter.
AI.method: Generate waveforms for detectable lensed massive-black-hole-binary population over a 4-year LISA mission; fit every signal with a smooth singular-isothermal-ellipsoid lens with external shear; analyze residuals after subtracting the smooth lens model to distinguish NFW, SIDM, and FDM structures.
AI.result: 132 lens systems produce 311 time-resolved images. NFW and SIDM produce real waveform changes but are largely degenerate with smooth lens parameters. FDM's coherent density fluctuations leave larger frequency-dependent residuals, making NFW-FDM and SIDM-FDM populations distinguishable with about 60 and 110 resolved image waveforms respectively.
AI.conclusion: Repeated lensed LISA signals can probe the spatial form of dark matter in lens galaxies, not just total lensing mass, with FDM being more distinguishable than NFW or SIDM due to its distinctive frequency-dependent phase signatures.

title: The role of filaments in the large-scale conformity signal
comment: 20 pages, 15 figures. Revised version submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: We investigate the large-scale conformity signal and its connection with the large-scale structure, focusing on low-mass central galaxies, after excluding galaxies that were satellites in the past. We measure the signal across different environments identified with the DisPerSE algorithm, including group outskirts, cluster outskirts, filaments, filament outskirts, and other environments (voids and walls) in order to assess how each population contributes to the large-scale conformity signal. We use the galaxy catalogs from the IllustrisTNG300 simulation and the semi-analytic model MDPL2-SAG. In SAG, galaxies embedded in filamentary regions emerge as the primary contributors to the large-scale conformity signal, closely reproducing its overall shape and amplitude. In TNG300, galaxies located in filamentary regions also exhibit a coherent, albeit weaker, conformity signal once galaxies that were satellites in the past are excluded. We also examine whether the signal depends on the adopted filament definition. We find no substantial differences when varying the filament thickness or considering galaxies in overlapping regions. Instead, the signal remains strong and largely insensitive to these differences. We then investigate the dependence of the conformity signal on filament linear density, length, and mass. The signal is enhanced in high-linear density, short, and high-mass filaments, but remains present in low-linear density, long, and low-mass filaments, although with a slightly lower amplitude. Finally, we find that low-mass central galaxies located in close proximity to interacting massive systems show an amplified conformity signal extending up to 4 Mpc/h. Overall, our results indicate that filamentary regions, and the tidal forces from neighboring massive systems play a fundamental role in shaping the large-scale conformity signal.

AI.tldr: Large-scale conformity signal is primarily driven by low-mass central galaxies in filamentary regions, with tidal forces from nearby massive systems amplifying the effect. The signal is robust to filament definition but depends on filament properties like linear density, length, and mass.
AI.motivation: To understand the origin of the large-scale conformity signal by examining its connection to large-scale structure (filaments, clusters, voids) after removing past satellites, and identifying which environments contribute most to the signal.
AI.method: Measured conformity signal across environments (group/cluster outskirts, filaments, filament outskirts, voids, walls) using DisPerSE algorithm on IllustrisTNG300 and MDPL2-SAG galaxy catalogs. Tested filament definition variations and dependence on filament properties (linear density, length, mass). Also examined proximity effects to massive systems.
AI.result: Filamentary regions dominate the conformity signal; SAG reproduces the signal well, TNG300 shows weaker but coherent signal. Signal is insensitive to filament definition/thickness. Enhanced in high-density, short, massive filaments. Proximity to massive systems amplifies signal up to 4 Mpc/h.
AI.conclusion: Filamentary regions and tidal forces from neighboring massive systems are fundamental drivers of the large-scale conformity signal.

title: A charge-flow instability in plasmas with charge fluctuations
summary: We present a linear instability in magnetized plasmas with charge fluctuations. It is driven by an electric current proportional to the charge chemical potential $μ$ and the bulk velocity. This charge-flow (C-flow) instability has hitherto not been considered in standard magnetohydrodynamics or its chiral extensions. We derive its dispersion relation and maximum growth rate, and confirm them with direct numerical simulations. We also show that the C-flow instability persists even for zero-mean fluctuations of $μ$, vanishing resistivity, and a magnetic Prandtl number of unity.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a novel linear instability called "charge-flow (C-flow) instability" in magnetized plasmas with charge fluctuations, driven by an electric current proportional to the charge chemical potential and bulk velocity. The authors derive the dispersion relation and growth rate, validated via numerical simulations, and show the instability persists under conditions of zero-mean chemical potential fluctuations, vanishing resistivity, and unity magnetic Prandtl number.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to identify and characterize a previously unrecognized linear instability in magnetized plasmas with charge fluctuations, which has been overlooked in standard magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and chiral MHD frameworks. This instability is driven by charge chemical potential and bulk velocity, filling a gap in plasma instability theory.
AI.method: The authors analytically derived the dispersion relation and maximum growth rate of the C-flow instability. They validated their theoretical predictions using direct numerical simulations (DNS). Key parameters considered include charge chemical potential fluctuations, resistivity, and magnetic Prandtl number.
AI.result: The C-flow instability exists and its dispersion relation and maximum growth rate are confirmed numerically. The instability persists even under extreme conditions: zero-mean fluctuations of the chemical potential, vanishing resistivity, and a magnetic Prandtl number of unity.
AI.conclusion: The C-flow instability is a distinct, robust linear instability in magnetized plasmas with charge fluctuations, not captured by standard MHD or chiral extensions. It may have implications for plasma dynamics in astrophysical and laboratory settings where charge fluctuations are relevant.

title: A quasar hatching from a buried red phase at z = 3.7
comment: 26 pages, 5 main figures, and 10 Extended Data figures. Submitted, comments are welcome
summary: We present JADES-GS 209777, previously cataloged as CANDELS J033238.02-274626.2, hereafter "the Hatchling," a red quasar at $z=3.711$. While the source has been reported in earlier deep-field catalogs, our multiwavelength analysis reveals a visible active nucleus still embedded in a dense gas- and dust-rich environment. Red quasar continua are often attributed to dust attenuation, including non-standard extinction curves, but the highly comprehensive multiwavelength data for this source provide direct constraints on the material being cleared. Using JWST/NIRSpec, NIRCam, MIRI, HST, MUSE, Chandra, ALMA, and VLA data, we detect broad emission lines and strong X-ray emission, showing that the active nucleus is at least partially exposed. We also detect H$α$ and He I absorption, indicating dense gas close to the nucleus. Kinematically disturbed O I, Mg II, Na D, and [O III] features, together with extended Ly$α$ emission over $\gtrsim 20$ kpc, further show that multiphase gas is being accelerated from the nuclear region into the host-galaxy environment. The ALMA detection reveals strong dust emission, with the inferred infrared luminosity placing the system in the ULIRG regime. The continuum is red and sharply declining toward the rest-frame UV, resembling compact red AGNs, and may reflect extreme dust attenuation, gas reprocessing, possible BAL-like absorption, or a combination of these effects. Regardless of which mechanism dominates the continuum shape, the line diagnostics show that the visible nucleus remains partially obscured by nearby material. The Hatchling therefore represents a unique opportunity to explore a poorly known transition phase in which feedback is likely clearing an enshrouded quasar and allowing it to emerge toward a more unobscured active nucleus.

AI.tldr: JADES-GS 209777 ("the Hatchling") is a red quasar at z=3.711 showing a partially exposed active nucleus still embedded in dense gas and dust, with evidence of multiphase outflows and feedback clearing the obscuring material, representing a transitional phase toward an unobscured quasar.
AI.motivation: To study a rare transitional phase where an enshrouded quasar is being cleared of its surrounding gas and dust, providing insight into the evolution from obscured to unobscured active galactic nuclei and the role of feedback in this process.
AI.method: Multiwavelength analysis using JWST/NIRSpec, NIRCam, MIRI, HST, MUSE, Chandra, ALMA, and VLA data to characterize the quasar's spectral features, dust emission, and kinematic signatures across multiple phases.
AI.result: Detected broad emission lines and strong X-ray emission (partially exposed AGN); Hα and He I absorption (dense nuclear gas); kinematically disturbed O I, Mg II, Na D, [O III]; extended Lyα over >20 kpc; ALMA shows ULIRG-level dust emission; red continuum declining toward rest-UV resembling compact red AGNs.
AI.conclusion: The Hatchling is in a poorly understood transition phase where feedback is clearing an enshrouded quasar, allowing it to emerge as a more unobscured active nucleus.

title: Relativistic Chiral MHD with application to the early Universe
summary: We present a systematic derivation of the equations of relativistic chiral magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) for a plasma of charged fermions in an expanding universe. Through a combination of a coordinate transformation and a rescaling of the dynamical variables, we bring the full system to the same form as in the Minkowski metric, with the Hubble expansion surviving only in the chirality-flipping rate and the kinematic viscosity. Retaining all four contributions to both the electric and the axial current yields terms absent from standard chiral MHD: charge-density corrections to the evolution equations for the chemical potentials, and an electric current proportional to the charge chemical potential $μ$ and the bulk velocity. The latter is mandated by current conservation, requires no chirality imbalance, and drives the charge-flow instability studied in a companion paper. For the radiation-dominated era, we evaluate all the coefficients in physical units and use them to estimate the magnetic Reynolds number, the attainable magnetic field strength, and the minimum temperature at which the chiral dynamo can operate. The resulting equations are cast in a form ready for direct numerical implementation.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically derives the equations of relativistic chiral magnetohydrodynamics for charged fermions in an expanding universe, showing that the system reduces to Minkowski form (with Hubble expansion only in chirality-flipping rate and viscosity) via coordinate transformation and rescaling. It includes charge-density corrections and a new electric current term driving charge-flow instability, and provides coefficient estimates for the radiation-dominated era.
AI.motivation: To systematically derive the full set of relativistic chiral MHD equations for charged fermions in an expanding universe, including all four contributions to electric and axial currents, which yield previously neglected terms such as charge-density corrections and a velocity-proportional electric current mandated by current conservation.
AI.method: The derivation uses a coordinate transformation and rescaling of dynamical variables to map the expanding universe system to Minkowski-space form, with Hubble expansion effects retained only in the chirality-flipping rate and kinematic viscosity. All four contributions to electric and axial currents are retained.
AI.result: The full system reduces to the Minkowski metric form; new terms emerge including charge-density corrections to chemical potential evolution equations and a μ-dependent electric current proportional to bulk velocity (driving charge-flow instability). Coefficients are evaluated for the radiation-dominated era, and estimates are provided for magnetic Reynolds number, attainable magnetic field strength, and minimum temperature for chiral dynamo operation.
AI.conclusion: The derived equations are cast in a form ready for direct numerical implementation, providing a complete framework for studying chiral MHD in expanding universes with all necessary physical coefficients estimated for the radiation-dominated era.

title: PhotoIFU: NIRCam as a Photometric Integral Field Unit for Mapping Feedback in Galaxies
comment: 22 pages. Submitted to ApJ. The code will be made publicly available
summary: We present PhotoIFU, a workflow that uses deep multi-band imaging as a low-resolution photometric integral field unit. Applied to PSF-matched JWST/NIRCam imaging, PhotoIFU treats each spatial pixel as a coarse SED element and fits the pixel SEDs with Prospector to map resolved stellar-population and ISM-related properties. We apply this approach to three galaxies at $z=1.3$--3.7 in JADES: two systems with extended ionized line emission and one post-starburst galaxy with an exceptionally strong neutral outflow. Pixel-by-pixel SED fitting gives maps of stellar-mass surface density, specific star formation rate, dust attenuation, gas-phase metallicity, and recent star-formation history. We find that regions selected from the extended-emission or outflow geometry occupy distinct parts of the resolved SED-property distribution compared with the full host. In the systems with extended ionized emission, these regions are generally less dusty, consistent with ionized emission being observed along dust-poor, low-column-density pathways through the host. In the neutral-outflow system, the selected regions show enhanced recent star formation, suggesting that compact rejuvenation may mark the aftermath of an earlier energetic phase. These results show that galactic outflows and extended emission-line structures can be spatially associated with measurable differences in resolved host-galaxy stellar populations and ISM-related properties. PhotoIFU provides an imaging-based method for resolved SED mapping of feedback-related structures in larger galaxy samples where full spectroscopic integral-field mapping is unavailable.

AI.tldr: PhotoIFU uses deep multi-band JWST/NIRCam imaging as a low-resolution photometric IFU, fitting pixel-by-pixel SEDs with Prospector to map resolved stellar-population and ISM properties in three high-z galaxies, revealing that extended emission-line and outflow regions occupy distinct parts of the resolved property distributions (less dusty or enhanced star formation).
AI.motivation: To develop an imaging-based method for resolved SED mapping of feedback-related structures (galactic outflows, extended emission-line regions) in large galaxy samples where full spectroscopic integral-field unit (IFU) data are unavailable.
AI.method: PSF-matched JWST/NIRCam multi-band imaging is treated as a low-resolution photometric IFU. Each spatial pixel is fitted as a coarse SED element using Prospector, yielding pixel-by-pixel maps of stellar-mass surface density, sSFR, dust attenuation, gas-phase metallicity, and recent star-formation history.
AI.result: In two systems with extended ionized emission, the selected regions are less dusty than the host, consistent with low-column-density pathways. In one post-starburst galaxy with a strong neutral outflow, the selected regions show enhanced recent star formation, suggesting compact rejuvenation after an earlier energetic phase.
AI.conclusion: Galactic outflows and extended emission-line structures are spatially associated with measurable differences in resolved host-galaxy stellar populations and ISM properties. PhotoIFU enables such analysis in larger samples without full spectroscopic IFU coverage.

title: Stability in Axion Inflation with Strong Backreaction from a Massive Vector Boson
summary: We study a modification of the model of axion inflation coupled to a $U(1)$ gauge field where the vector field is massive. In the conventional scenario with a massless gauge field, the onset of the regime where the gauge field strongly backreacts on the inflaton displays an instability whose nonlinear evolution and endpoint remain poorly understood. We argue that, if the gauge field is massive enough, the transition to the strong backreaction regime instead occurs smoothly, avoiding this instability. This observation suggests that axion inflation with massive gauge fields admits a controllable strong backreaction regime, so that a phenomenologically viable realization of inflation might be possible in this class of models.

AI.tldr: Axion inflation with a massive U(1) gauge field avoids the instability seen in the massless case, allowing a controllable strong backreaction regime that may yield phenomenologically viable inflation.
AI.motivation: In standard axion inflation with a massless gauge field, the transition to strong backreaction leads to an instability whose nonlinear evolution is poorly understood, motivating the study of a massive gauge field as a way to circumvent this issue.
AI.method: The authors analyze a modified axion inflation model where the U(1) gauge field is massive, comparing its dynamics to the conventional massless case, particularly focusing on the onset and behavior of the strong backreaction regime.
AI.result: A sufficiently massive gauge field allows the transition to strong backreaction to occur smoothly, avoiding the instability present in the massless scenario.
AI.conclusion: Axion inflation with massive gauge fields can support a controllable strong backreaction regime, potentially enabling a phenomenologically viable realization of inflation in this class of models.

title: HETDEX: Star Formation Stochasticity Diagram of Lyman Alpha Emitting Galaxies at Cosmic Noon Confirms Three Archetypes
summary: In this work, we aim to measure the star formation stochasticity of Lyman Alpha Emitting Galaxies (LAEs) at Cosmic Noon. We identify 270 LAEs from the HETDEX Survey in the COSMOS field with rest-UV-through-NIR photometry from CANDELS\null. For each LAE, we perform non-parametric gaussian-process star formation history (SFH) reconstruction using the Dense Basis method. Our HETDEX LAE sample is described well by the three SFH archetypes defined for ODIN LAEs in Firestone et al. 2025 with comparable frequency: First Burst, Dominant Burst, and Nondominant Burst. The rapidly rising Star Formation Rates (SFRs) of First Burst LAEs are not adequately represented in traditional SFR$_{100}-M_*$ diagrams, where SFR$_{100}$ is averaged over the most recent 100Myr. This motivates the usage of SFR$_{10}-M_*$, where SFR$_{10}$ is averaged over the most recent 10Myr. We introduce the Star Formation Stochasticity Diagram, a diagnostic tool that probes variations in galaxies' SFRs across cosmic time. By eliminating the confounding factor of redshift evolution, we are able to employ a gaussian mixture model to decompose our ratio of short- vs.long-term SFR into statistically motivated sub-populations. This agnostic component decomposition reveals three populations consistent with the empirical LAE SFH archetypes. We can, therefore, summarize the overall stellar mass assembly of LAEs with this ratio, even without viewing their full star formation histories.

AI.tldr: A study of 270 HETDEX LAEs at Cosmic Noon using Dense Basis SFH reconstruction introduces the Star Formation Stochasticity Diagram based on SFR₁₀/SFR₁₀₀ ratios, identifying three SFH archetypes (First Burst, Dominant Burst, Nondominant Burst) and demonstrating that this ratio summarizes stellar mass assembly without full SFH reconstruction.
AI.motivation: To measure the star formation stochasticity of Lyman Alpha Emitting Galaxies at Cosmic Noon and develop a diagnostic tool that probes variations in galaxies' star formation rates across cosmic time, addressing the inadequacy of traditional SFR₁₀₀-M* diagrams for rapidly rising SFRs.
AI.method: The authors identified 270 LAEs from the HETDEX Survey in the COSMOS field with rest-UV-through-NIR photometry from CANDELS, performed non-parametric Gaussian-process star formation history reconstruction using the Dense Basis method, and introduced a Star Formation Stochasticity Diagram using SFR₁₀/SFR₁₀₀ ratios. A Gaussian mixture model was employed for agnostic component decomposition into sub-populations.
AI.result: The HETDEX LAE sample is well described by three SFH archetypes (First Burst, Dominant Burst, Nondominant Burst) with comparable frequency to ODIN LAEs. The SFR₁₀-M* diagram better represents First Burst LAEs. The Gaussian mixture model on SFR ratio data yielded three statistically motivated sub-populations consistent with these archetypes.
AI.conclusion: The authors demonstrate that LAE star formation histories can be summarized by the ratio of short-term (10 Myr) to long-term (100 Myr) star formation rates, using a Star Formation Stochasticity Diagram with a Gaussian mixture model to identify three SFH archetypes (First Burst, Dominant Burst, Nondominant Burst) consistent with empirical classifications, enabling characterization of stellar mass assembly without full SFH reconstruction.

title: Measurement of All-sky Neutral hydrogen Absorption Spectrum (MANAS)
summary:
MANAS is a single antenna, ground-based platform built to measure the sky averaged ('global') redshifted 21-cm signal from Cosmic Dawn. The cosmological signal is expected as a ~ 100-200 mK absorption trough against a foreground of 3-4 orders of magnitude brighter. The current crop of 21-cm experiments are limited by systematics namely the sky, ionosphere, beam, and signal path effects.
  MANAS combines an achromatic monopole antenna, an absolutely-calibrated receiver, and in-situ beam mapping with the OVRO-LWA, and develops an end-to-end error budget that quantifies each systematic.

AI.tldr: MANAS is a ground-based platform using a single antenna to measure the global 21-cm signal from Cosmic Dawn, addressing systematics through an achromatic monopole, absolute calibration, in-situ beam mapping, and an end-to-end error budget.
AI.motivation: To measure the faint sky-averaged 21-cm absorption signal (~100-200 mK) from Cosmic Dawn, which is buried under foregrounds 3-4 orders of magnitude brighter, and to overcome systematic limitations from the sky, ionosphere, beam, and signal path effects that plague current experiments.
AI.method: Combines an achromatic monopole antenna, an absolutely-calibrated receiver, and in-situ beam mapping using the OVRO-LWA, along with a quantified end-to-end error budget for each systematic.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the paper describes the system design and error budget approach rather than specific measured results.
AI.conclusion: MANAS addresses key systematic limitations in global 21-cm experiments through combined achromatic antenna design, absolute calibration, in-situ beam mapping, and comprehensive error budgeting.

title: Correlation between the two-armed $V_R$ spiral in the $Z$--$V_Z$ plane and moving groups
summary:
We use a cross-matched sample of 3.7 million stars from Gaia DR3 and LAMOST DR7 to investigate the velocity substructures in the Milky Way disk. The median radial velocity $V_R$ as a function of guiding-center radius $R_g$ exhibits alternating positive and negative stripes, which are strongly correlated with known moving groups. By examining the $V_R$ distribution in the $Z$--$V_Z$ phase space, we find that the D1, P2, D2, and P3 $V_R$ stripes display clear two-armed spirals.
  Among the moving groups embedded in these $V_R$ stripes, the Coma Berenices moving group in the P3 stripe exhibits the most pronounced two-armed spiral and serves as the primary contributor to the left arm of the overall P3 spiral. The angular momentum, eccentricities, orbital frequencies, and frequency ratios of its stars are consistent with either the corotation resonance of the spiral arms or the $m=4$ inner Lindblad resonance of the bar.
  Test-particle simulations confirm that a bar with a varying pattern speed, together with static or transient spiral arms, can produce such two-armed spirals.

AI.tldr: Using 3.7M Gaia DR3 and LAMOST DR7 stars, we find alternating V_R stripes in the Milky Way disk correlated with moving groups. The D1, P2, D2, P3 stripes show two-armed spirals in Z-V_Z space, with the Coma Berenices group in P3 being the most prominent. Its orbital properties align with spiral arm corotation resonance or bar's m=4 inner Lindblad resonance. Simulations show a varying-speed bar with spiral arms can produce these spirals.
AI.motivation: To investigate velocity substructures in the Milky Way disk and understand their dynamical origins using large-scale astrometric and spectroscopic data.
AI.method: Cross-matched 3.7M stars from Gaia DR3 and LAMOST DR7; analyzed median V_R as function of R_g; examined V_R distribution in Z-V_Z phase space; performed test-particle simulations with bar and spiral arm models.
AI.result: Discovered alternating positive/negative V_R stripes correlated with moving groups; D1/P2/D2/P3 stripes show clear two-armed spirals; Coma Berenices group in P3 stripe exhibits the most pronounced two-armed spiral and is the main contributor to the P3 spiral's left arm.
AI.conclusion: The observed two-armed spirals can be produced by a bar with a varying pattern speed combined with static or transient spiral arms, with the Coma Berenices group's orbital properties consistent with either corotation resonance of spiral arms or m=4 inner Lindblad resonance of the bar.

title: Interpreting the stacked kinetic SZ effect I: velocity reconstruction and non-linear velocity effects
summary: The stacked kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ) signal probes the velocity-weighted projected gas momentum around galaxies, and is emerging as a powerful probe of gas fractions and baryonic feedback. Its interpretation, however, rests on several assumptions that we test in this pair of companion papers. Using the FLAMINGO hydrodynamical simulations and DESI-like galaxy mocks for luminous red galaxies (LRGs), the bright galaxy sample (BGS), and emission-line galaxies (ELGs), we identify the ingredients required to model the signal to better than $10\%$. This first paper focuses on velocities. We decompose the signal into a dominant bulk-flow term, proportional to the mean optical depth, plus non-linear terms arising from the small-scale gas momentum and its coupling to the stacking velocity. When the stacking velocities are reconstructed from linear information in real space alone -- an idealisation which is not possible in practice -- the non-linear terms cancel and the signal traces the mean optical depth to within a few per cent. When the stacking velocity instead retains non-linear information or is affected by redshift-space distortions, the non-linear terms suppress the signal by $10-20\%$: a $1-2σ$ effect for current data that is expected to be statistically significant for upcoming surveys, and one that depends only weakly on baryonic feedback. Our results reveal a trade-off: velocity estimators that retain small-scale information boost signal-to-noise but require simulation-based modelling, whereas conservative reconstructions simplify the interpretation at the cost of signal-to-noise.

AI.tldr: This paper uses FLAMINGO simulations to test assumptions in the stacked kSZ effect, finding that while idealized linear velocity reconstructions yield clean signals tracing mean optical depth, non-linearities and redshift-space distortions in realistic velocity estimators suppress the signal by 10-20%, creating a trade-off between signal-to-noise and interpretability.
AI.motivation: The stacked kSZ signal is emerging as a powerful probe of gas fractions and baryonic feedback, but its interpretation rests on several untested assumptions that need verification to ensure accurate modeling.
AI.method: Using FLAMINGO hydrodynamical simulations with DESI-like galaxy mocks (LRGs, BGS, ELGs), the authors decompose the kSZ signal into dominant bulk-flow and non-linear terms, testing how different velocity reconstruction methods affect the signal.
AI.result: Idealized linear velocity reconstructions yield signals tracing mean optical depth to within a few percent, but realistic reconstructions with non-linear information or redshift-space distortions suppress the signal by 10-20%, a 1-2σ effect for current data expected to be significant for upcoming surveys.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental trade-off: velocity estimators retaining small-scale information increase signal-to-noise but require simulation-based modeling, while conservative reconstructions simplify interpretation at the cost of signal-to-noise.

title: X-ray disc reverberation modelling of the X-ray/UV/optical spectral/timing properties of Fairall 9
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Multiwavelength monitoring surveys of active galactic nuclei (AGN) have revealed correlated variability observed in the X-ray, UV, and optical bands. X-ray reverberation, arising from the absorption of X-rays illuminating the accretion disc, provides a self-consistent physical framework for interpreting these observations and imposing constraints on the geometry and energetics of accretion flows and X-ray coronae. We aim to apply the X-ray disc reverberation framework to the Seyfert 1 galaxy Fairall 9, a well-studied AGN with a clear line of sight to the accretion disc, to investigate whether this physical scenario can simultaneously account for its observed spectral and timing properties, as probed by its mean spectral energy distribution (SED), UV/optical power spectral densities (PSDs), and interband time lags. We used multiwavelength data from the 2018-2021 Swift intensive monitoring campaign to construct the mean X-ray/UV/optical SED and to compute PSDs in all bands. We first modelled the broadband average SED using KYNSED, which is a physical X-ray reverberation model assuming lamp-post geometry. The resulting best-fit parameter space was then used to model the UV/optical PSDs and further constrain the physical parameters of the system. Finally, we tested whether the observed interband time lags are consistent with the model predictions for the parameter sets that simultaneously reproduce both the SED and the PSDs. X-ray illumination of the accretion disc can explain the broadband mean SED of Fairall 9. The UV/optical variations are likely driven by the variable X-rays that illuminate the disc, and not by short-timescale disc fluctuations of unknown physical origin. X-ray disc illumination and reverberation can explain the mean energy spectrum, the UV/optical power spectra, and the wavelength-dependent time lags simultaneously for a common set of physical parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper applies X-ray disc reverberation modeling to the Seyfert 1 galaxy Fairall 9, showing that X-ray illumination of the accretion disc can simultaneously explain its mean SED, UV/optical PSDs, and interband time lags observed during a 2018-2021 Swift monitoring campaign.
AI.motivation: To test whether the X-ray disc reverberation framework can self-consistently account for the observed spectral and timing properties (SED, PSDs, interband lags) of Fairall 9, a well-studied AGN with a clear view of its accretion disc.
AI.method: Multiwavelength Swift data (2018-2021) were used to construct mean SED and PSDs. The SED was modeled with KYNSED (a lamp-post X-ray reverberation model). Best-fit parameters from the SED were used to model UV/optical PSDs, and the consistency with observed interband time lags was then tested.
AI.result: X-ray illumination of the accretion disc explains the broadband mean SED. UV/optical variability is driven by variable X-ray illumination rather than intrinsic disc fluctuations. A common set of physical parameters simultaneously reproduces the SED, PSDs, and wavelength-dependent time lags.
AI.conclusion: X-ray disc reverberation provides a self-consistent physical explanation for the correlated multiwavelength variability in Fairall 9, supporting the lamp-post geometry and X-ray reprocessing as the origin of UV/optical variability in AGN.

title: The Degree of Fine-Tuning Needed for a Viable Universe: Not Fragile?
comment: 79 pages, 16 figures, to appear in the FQxI Foundational Review Series
summary: (abridged) In order for the universe to develop astrophysical structures and support life, the fundamental constants that determine the laws of physics and the cosmological parameters that specify cosmic properties must fall within a range of values. The goal of this review is to delineate these ranges. We start with the premise that multiple universes can exist and can sample different realizations of the laws of physics. This treatment focuses on the coupling constants that determine the strength of the fundamental forces $(α,α_G,α_{\rm s},α_{\rm w})$ and the masses of the particles $(m_u,m_d,m_e)$ that make up atomic matter. We also consider cosmological parameters, including the energy density parameter $Ω$, the dark energy density $ρ_v$, the baryon-to-photon ratio $η$, the dark matter contribution $δ$, the amplitude $Q$ of primordial density fluctuations, and the number ${\cal D}$ of spatial dimensions. These quantities are constrained by the need for the universe to emerge from its epoch of nucleosynthesis with an acceptable chemical composition, live for a long time, and ultimately produce galaxies, stars, and planets. Stellar lifetimes must be long enough and surface temperatures must be high enough to support life. These requirements place constraints on the fundamental constants and cosmological parameters. This overview discusses several classic instances of possible fine-tuning in stars, including the triple alpha reaction, stable diprotons, and unstable deuterium. Finally, we note that for universes with significantly different parameters, a variety of astrophysical processes can generate energy, drive nucleosynthesis, and potentially support habitability.

AI.tldr: This review examines the range of fundamental constants (coupling strengths α, α_G, α_s, α_w; particle masses m_u, m_d, m_e) and cosmological parameters (Ω, ρ_v, η, δ, Q, D) required for the universe to form astrophysical structures and support life. It assumes a multiverse framework, constrains parameters by nucleosynthesis, long-term cosmic evolution, galaxy/star/planet formation, stellar lifetimes, and habitability. Classic fine-tuning examples (triple alpha, diprotons, deuterium) are discussed, noting alternative habitability pathways in universes with different parameters.
AI.motivation: To systematically delineate the range of fundamental constants and cosmological parameters that allow a universe to develop astrophysical structures and support life, under the premise that multiple universes may sample different laws of physics.
AI.method: The review sets constraints on coupling constants (α, α_G, α_s, α_w), particle masses (m_u, m_d, m_e), and cosmological parameters (Ω, ρ_v, η, δ, Q, D) by requiring successful nucleosynthesis, long-lived cosmic evolution, galaxy/star/planet formation, sufficient stellar lifetimes and surface temperatures for habitability. Classic fine-tuning cases (triple alpha reaction, diprotons, deuterium stability) are examined.
AI.result: Delineated ranges for fundamental constants and cosmological parameters required for a life-supporting universe; identification of classic fine-tuning instances (triple alpha, diprotons, deuterium); recognition that universes with significantly different parameters can still generate energy, nucleosynthesis, and potential habitability through alternative astrophysical processes.
AI.conclusion: The fundamental constants and cosmological parameters are constrained within specific ranges to produce a universe capable of supporting life; however, alternative parameter regimes may still permit habitability through different astrophysical pathways, reducing the apparent fine-tuning requirement.

title: The ALMA-QUARKS Survey: Properties of Hot Molecular Fragments in the Massive Protocluster IRAS 17233-3606
summary: To investigate the physical mechanisms of fragmentation within the hot molecular core of the massive protocluster IRAS 17233-3606 (G351.78-0.54), we carried out a detailed analysis of continuum and lines, using the ALMA Band 3 data from the ATOMS survey and Band 6 data from the QUARKS survey. The low-resolution 3 mm data reveal a massive hot core MM1 with a mass of ~81.3 Msun, and a prominent ultracompact (UC) HII region MM2, while the high-resolution data resolve MM1 into 11 hot molecular fragments (HMFs). These HMFs exhibit hot (Trot = 100-310 K) CH3CN and CH3OH emission and high column densities (NH2 > 10^23 cm^-2), indicating their potential to form massive stars. Based on outflows, masers, HII regions, and f[CH3CN/CH3O] abundance ratios, the evolutionary sequences of the 11 HMFs are categorized as phases I to IV. The mean minimum-spanning tree (MST) separation (~1.8 x 10^3 au) of the HMFs is nearly half of the thermal Jeans length (~3.3 x 10^3 au). Together with the Q parameter Q = 0.77 and virial parameter alpha_vir = 0.84 of MM1, these results suggest an evolutionary scenario in which fragmentation is initially driven by thermal instability, followed by global gravitational contraction and growth through active accretion. Meanwhile, feedback from the B2-type zero-age main-sequence (ZAMS) star and the UC HII region significantly influence the morphology and chemical properties of MM1 and MM2. This heterogeneity highlights the role of diverse physical processes taking place in high-mass protoclusters.

AI.tldr: A detailed ALMA study of the hot molecular core IRAS 17233-3606 resolves 11 hot molecular fragments (HMFs) within the massive protocluster. Fragmentation is initially driven by thermal instability, followed by gravitational contraction and accretion. Feedback from a B2-type ZAMS star and UC HII region shapes the morphology and chemistry.
AI.motivation: To investigate the physical mechanisms of fragmentation within the hot molecular core of the massive protocluster IRAS 17233-3606 (G351.78-0.54).
AI.method: Analysis of ALMA Band 3 (ATOMS survey) and Band 6 (QUARKS survey) continuum and line data, including low-resolution (3 mm) and high-resolution observations. Used CH3CN and CH3OH emission to derive rotational temperatures and column densities. Applied MST (minimum-spanning tree) separation, Q parameter, and virial parameter analysis. Classified evolutionary phases via outflows, masers, HII regions, and abundance ratios.
AI.result: Low-res data reveal a massive hot core MM1 (~81.3 Msun) and a UC HII region MM2. High-res data resolve MM1 into 11 HMFs with hot gas (Trot=100-310 K) and high column densities (NH2 > 10^23 cm^-2). Mean MST separation (~1.8e3 au) is half the thermal Jeans length (~3.3e3 au); Q=0.77, alpha_vir=0.84. The 11 HMFs are categorized into evolutionary phases I-IV.
AI.conclusion: Fragmentation is initially driven by thermal instability, followed by global gravitational contraction and active accretion. Feedback from the B2-type ZAMS star and UC HII region significantly influences the morphology and chemical properties, highlighting the role of diverse physical processes in high-mass protoclusters.

title: Cosmological perturbations and clustering mechanisms in multifield dark energy
summary: We investigate the cosmological signatures of two-field dark energy with curved field-space geometry. We numerically solve the background and linear perturbation equations and assess the validity of the effective single-field description. We examine three distinct dark-energy clustering mechanisms: effective sound-speed suppression, dynamical excitation of the heavy mode, and tachyonic instabilities induced by field-space curvature, and explore their possible imprints on the matter power spectrum and cosmic microwave background anisotropies. Our analysis establishes multifield dark energy as a rich and testable extension of quintessence, with observable clustering signatures relevant to current and future cosmological surveys.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates two-field dark energy models with curved field-space geometry, solving background and linear perturbation equations to assess when the effective single-field description breaks down. It identifies three clustering mechanisms—sound-speed suppression, heavy-mode excitation, and tachyonic instabilities—and studies their imprints on the matter power spectrum and CMB anisotropies, establishing multifield dark energy as a testable extension of quintessence.
AI.motivation: To explore whether multifield dark energy with curved field-space geometry produces distinct observable cosmological signatures beyond the standard single-field quintessence description, and to assess the validity of effective single-field approximations.
AI.method: Numerical solution of background and linear perturbation equations for two-field dark energy models with curved field-space geometry, analyzing three clustering mechanisms (effective sound-speed suppression, dynamical excitation of heavy mode, tachyonic instabilities) and their effects on the matter power spectrum and CMB anisotropies.
AI.result: The effective single-field description can break down in curved field-space scenarios. Three distinct clustering mechanisms produce observable signatures: sound-speed suppression alters perturbation growth, heavy-mode excitation introduces additional dynamics, and field-space-curvature-induced tachyonic instabilities further modify clustering. These effects leave imprints on both the matter power spectrum and CMB anisotropies.
AI.conclusion: Multifield dark energy with curved field-space geometry is a rich, testable extension of quintessence that produces observable clustering signatures relevant to current and future cosmological surveys, motivating further observational searches for beyond-single-field effects in dark energy.

title: Disc Candidates in IC 2395: A WISE Survey of the Kinematically Confirmed Membership
summary: Circumstellar disc dissipation timescales constrain the window available for planet formation. At approximately 9 Myr, IC 2395 lies at a critical epoch in primordial disc evolution, yet no kinematically selected disc census exists beyond the inner cluster core. A wide-field survey of IC 2395, extending to a 2 degree radius, establishes a kinematically selected disc census and evaluates the frequency of planet-forming environments in the outer cluster field. Using a high-purity catalogue of 173 members identified via Gaia DR3 kinematics, mid-infrared excesses are identified using AllWISE photometry. Candidates are classified into two tiers: Crossvalidated (corroborated by Gaia variability) and Single-band detections. Twenty-one disc candidates are identified, 90% of which lie beyond the footprint of prior Spitzer surveys. The candidates are concentrated among low-mass members (0.31-0.68M), with no significant correlation between mass and excess (Spearman rho = +0.07, p = 0.84). A secure disc fraction of 4.0 p/m 1.5% is established by the Cross-validated subsample, independently confirmed by Gaia DR3 YSO variability classification; a photometric 3 sigma significance cut yields a consistent estimate of 2.9 p/m 1.3%. An upper bound of 12.1 p/m 2.5% is derived from all 21 W1-W2 excess candidates, with a background subtracted value of approximately 10.1%. Gaia DR3 epoch photometry reveals diverse variability morphologies, including a dramatic dipper and multiple bursters, confirming ongoing magnetospheric accretion. By extending the survey radius, this work demonstrates that infrared excess sources indicative of inner-disc emission in IC 2395 are more abundant and widely distributed than previously recognised. The survival of these discs in the lower-density outer field provides a well-characterised sample for studying the final stages of disc evolution and planet formation.

AI.tldr: A wide-field kinematic survey of the ~9 Myr old cluster IC 2395 identifies 21 disc candidates, with 90% beyond prior surveys, yielding a disc fraction of 4.0±1.5% (cross-validated) to 12.1±2.5% (upper bound), demonstrating that inner-disc emission sources are more abundant and widely distributed in the outer cluster field than previously recognised.
AI.motivation: Circumstellar disc dissipation timescales constrain the window for planet formation, yet no kinematically selected disc census exists beyond the inner core of IC 2395, a cluster at the critical ~9 Myr epoch in primordial disc evolution.
AI.method: A high-purity catalogue of 173 members identified via Gaia DR3 kinematics; mid-infrared excesses identified using AllWISE photometry; candidates classified into Cross-validated (corroborated by Gaia variability) and Single-band detections; Gaia DR3 epoch photometry for variability morphology analysis.
AI.result: 21 disc candidates identified, 90% beyond prior Spitzer footprints; concentrated among low-mass members (0.31-0.68 M☉); no significant mass-excess correlation; disc fractions: 4.0±1.5% (cross-validated), 2.9±1.3% (3σ cut), 12.1±2.5% (upper bound), ~10.1% (background subtracted). Diverse variability morphologies (dipper, bursters) confirm ongoing magnetospheric accretion.
AI.conclusion: Infrared excess sources indicative of inner-disc emission in IC 2395 are more abundant and widely distributed than previously recognised; disc survival in the lower-density outer field provides a well-characterised sample for studying the final stages of disc evolution and planet formation.

title: Hermes - Towards an Optimal High-Performance Algorithm for Cosmic Statistics of Large Data Sets
comment: 45 pages, 18 figures, and 4 tables. Source code: https://github.com/SYSUSPA-Projects/PyHermes
summary: We present Hermes, an in situ multiresolution framework for efficient and flexible measurements of cosmic large-scale-structure statistics from discrete catalogues. Hermes reconstructs a catalogue as a continuous density field in a compact scaling-function basis and replaces explicit counting of particle tuples with algebraic operations among window-filtered fields. Standard binning schemes for counts-in-cells, two-point and higher-order correlation functions are thereby expressed through choices of window functions, while new statistics can be constructed by modifying the kernels without redesigning the estimator. We introduce PyHermes, an open-source Python implementation combining multiresolution reconstruction, FFT-based convolution, MPI/thread parallelism, and GPU acceleration. It supports isotropic and anisotropic two-point statistics, marked correlations, standard and multipole three-point functions, filtered statistics, and differential operators for derived physical fields. Tests with cosmological N-body halo catalogues demonstrate a range of clustering measurements and quantify the computational efficiency and scalability of the approach. By separating field representation from statistical windows, a single reconstructed field can be reused for many standard and customised measurements, making Hermes well suited to large data sets from current and future galaxy surveys.

AI.tldr: Hermes is an in situ multiresolution framework that reconstructs discrete catalogues as continuous density fields for efficient cosmic large-scale-structure measurements. Its open-source Python implementation (PyHermes) supports various statistical measurements via algebraic operations on window-filtered fields, with parallel and GPU acceleration, and is designed for reuse across standard and custom analyses.
AI.motivation: To enable efficient and flexible measurements of cosmic large-scale-structure statistics from discrete catalogues, avoiding redundant computation by separating field representation from statistical windows.
AI.method: Reconstructs catalogues as continuous density fields in a compact scaling-function basis, replaces explicit particle tuple counting with algebraic operations on window-filtered fields, and uses FFT-based convolution, MPI/thread parallelism, and GPU acceleration.
AI.result: Tests with cosmological N-body halo catalogues demonstrate a range of clustering measurements and quantify computational efficiency and scalability.
AI.conclusion: A single reconstructed field can be reused for many standard and customised measurements, making Hermes well suited to large data sets from current and future galaxy surveys.

title: On the Jeans criterion in hydrostatic stratified media
summary: The classical Jeans stability criterion neglects spatial gradients in background physical quantities such as density and pressure. Here, we revisit the Jeans analysis for a non-rotating fluid in hydrostatic equilibrium, explicitly accounting for these gradients and deriving a modified dispersion relation governing perturbation propagation. Using physical arguments, we show why the Jeans swindle is not required to derive the Jeans criterion for perturbations that are small compared to the size of the host system. We use linear perturbation analysis alongside an averaging procedure to study the behavior of the local Eulerian perturbations in a hydrostatic medium, showing that background gradients enter the dispersion relation in a highly non-trivial manner, precluding the derivation of a general gravitational stability criterion applicable to an arbitrary hydrostatic system. We demonstrate that, in the local short-wavelength limit, the standard Jeans criterion remains valid despite the presence of nonzero background gradients, and that all local perturbations in a hydrostatic system are stable against local gravitational collapse. We conclude that it is not possible to derive a general local gravitational stability criterion valid for an arbitrary hydrostatic background; however, in the local short-wavelength limit, the standard Jeans criterion remains valid.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits the Jeans stability criterion for a non-rotating fluid in hydrostatic equilibrium, explicitly accounting for background gradients (density, pressure) that classical Jeans analysis neglects. Using linear perturbation analysis and an averaging procedure, the authors show that background gradients complicate the dispersion relation, preventing a general local gravitational stability criterion. However, in the local short-wavelength limit, the standard Jeans criterion remains valid, and all local perturbations are stable against local gravitational collapse. The Jeans swindle is not required for small perturbations relative to system size.
AI.motivation: The classical Jeans stability criterion neglects spatial gradients in background physical quantities such as density and pressure. The authors aim to revisit the Jeans analysis for a non-rotating fluid in hydrostatic equilibrium by explicitly accounting for these gradients, addressing the limitations of the Jeans swindle.
AI.method: Linear perturbation analysis alongside an averaging procedure is used to study the behavior of local Eulerian perturbations in a hydrostatic medium. The analysis explicitly includes background gradients and derives a modified dispersion relation.
AI.result: Background gradients enter the dispersion relation in a highly non-trivial manner, precluding a general gravitational stability criterion for arbitrary hydrostatic systems. In the local short-wavelength limit, the standard Jeans criterion remains valid, and all local perturbations are stable against local gravitational collapse.
AI.conclusion: It is not possible to derive a general local gravitational stability criterion valid for an arbitrary hydrostatic background; however, in the local short-wavelength limit, the standard Jeans criterion remains valid. The Jeans swindle is not required for perturbations small compared to the host system size.

title: First Directional Dark Matter Limits from the MIMAC μ-TPC Detector
summary: We present a directional dark matter search using the MIMAC (Micro-tpc Matrix of Chambers) detector at the Modane Underground Laboratory. Operating a low-pressure gas mixture of i-C4H10 and 50% CHF3 at 30 mbar, without any shielding, the detector allows the reconstruction of the 3D tracks of nuclear recoils produced in the 6-liter active volume. Directionality is a crucial tool to discriminate true WIMP signals from those of background producing identical recoils, such as neutrons. We analyze data from two independent chambers with effective exposures of 495.1 and 354.2 days, respectively. To estimate the background directly from the data, we apply a standard ON/OFF spatial analysis. By projecting the reconstructed tracks onto the galactic map and applying a moving kinematic energy cut depending on the WIMP mass, we compare the event rate in the signal direction with multiple OFF-source regions. Finding no significant excess of events in the direction of the Cygnus constellation, we set an upper limit on the spin-dependent WIMP-protoncross section.

AI.tldr: The MIMAC directional dark matter search at Modane Underground Laboratory used a low-pressure gas detector to reconstruct 3D tracks of nuclear recoils. Analyzing data from two chambers with effective exposures of 495.1 and 354.2 days, and applying ON/OFF spatial analysis with kinematic energy cuts, they found no significant excess in the Cygnus direction and set an upper limit on the spin-dependent WIMP-proton cross section.
AI.motivation: Directional dark matter detection is motivated as a crucial tool to discriminate true WIMP signals from background neutrons that produce identical nuclear recoils, addressing a key challenge in direct dark matter searches.
AI.method: The experiment uses the MIMAC detector (Micro-tpc Matrix of Chambers) with a low-pressure gas mixture of i-C4H10 and 50% CHF3 at 30 mbar, without shielding, enabling 3D track reconstruction of nuclear recoils in a 6-liter active volume. The analysis applies ON/OFF spatial method for background estimation, projects reconstructed tracks onto galactic coordinates, applies moving kinematic energy cuts dependent on WIMP mass, and compares event rates in the signal direction (Cygnus constellation) with multiple OFF-source regions.
AI.result: No significant excess of events was observed in the direction of the Cygnus constellation relative to OFF-source regions.
AI.conclusion: An upper limit on the spin-dependent WIMP-proton cross section was set based on the null result from directional analysis.

title: Spatial Correlations of PAH, UV, H$α$ Emission and IMF - PAH Variations in the Star-Forming Complexes of NGC 628
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 15 pages, including references and appendix, 11 figures
summary: We examine the spatial correlation of emission from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH) (3.3 $μ$m, 7.7 $μ$m, and 11.3 $μ$m) with the far-ultraviolet (FUV), near-ultraviolet (NUV), and H$α$ emission from star-forming complexes (SFCs) in different regions of NGC 628. We use the James Webb Space Telescope to detect PAH emission, along with the Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope and Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer observations to sample the UV and H$α$ emission, respectively. We investigate the correlation of PAH luminosities with FUV, NUV, and H$α$ luminosities for the extracted SFCs. We find that the arm and spur SFCs show bright PAH emission, except for those with only NUV emission, located primarily in bubbles and superbubbles. We also examine these correlations in the phantom void, the largest superbubble in NGC 628. We investigate the trend for FUV-NUV and the Initial mass function (IMF) index $α_2$ derived from the ratio of B stars with PAH band ratios (F335M/F1130W, F770W/F1130W, and F335M/F770W). We find that PAH band ratios increase as the IMF becomes more top-heavy and the SFCs become bluer, consistent with enhanced PAH excitation and ionisation in stronger UV radiation fields. However, $α_2$ of spur SFCs shows a flat trend with PAH band ratios compared to arms. Upon closer examination, two SFCs in the shell region of the phantom void showed a flatter IMF compared to the SFC located near the elongated bubble. This is likely due to gas accumulation, possibly through feedback mechanisms in the shell region, while the SFC near the elongated bubble may have formed in a region affected by shear.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes PAH emission correlations with UV and Hα in star-forming complexes of NGC 628 using JWST, UVIT, and MUSE data, finding that PAH band ratios increase with top-heavier IMFs and bluer SFCs, with differences between arm and spur regions.
AI.motivation: To understand the spatial correlation between PAH emission (3.3, 7.7, 11.3 μm) and FUV, NUV, and Hα emission from star-forming complexes in NGC 628, and to investigate how PAH band ratios relate to the IMF slope and UV radiation field strength.
AI.method: JWST for PAH emission detection; UVIT for UV; MUSE for Hα; extraction of SFCs; correlation analysis of PAH luminosities with FUV, NUV, Hα; analysis of FUV-NUV colors and IMF index α₂ derived from B star ratios vs PAH band ratios (F335M/F1130W, F770W/F1130W, F335M/F770W).
AI.result: Arm and spur SFCs show bright PAH emission except those with only NUV emission in bubbles/superbubbles. PAH band ratios increase with top-heavier IMF and bluer SFCs. Spur SFCs show flatter α₂ trend vs PAH ratios compared to arms. Two SFCs in phantom void shell show flatter IMF than one near an elongated bubble.
AI.conclusion: Enhanced PAH excitation/ionization occurs in stronger UV fields. Gas accumulation via feedback in shell regions may flatten IMF, while shear-affected regions near elongated bubbles show different IMF characteristics.

title: Cosmic microwave background temperature cosmography
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables; letter published in MNRAS
summary: The temperature-redshift relation, $T(z)=T_0(1+z)$, is a cornerstone of the standard cosmological model, but it is violated in many physically motivated extensions thereof, e.g. when photon number is not conserved. We apply the methodology of cosmography, a model-independent approach to cosmology, to this observable, and use astrophysical Sunyaev-Zeldovich and high-resolution spectroscopic measurements spanning the redshift range $0\le z\le6.34$, to constrain violations of the standard relation. We explore the impact of different cosmographic approaches and expansion variable choices and also compare the cosmographic constraints with those obtained, with the same data, in the canonical adiabatic extension model of Lima. While these choices have some impact, overall we find that such violations are constrained to percent level, and that a single non-standard parameter suffices to describe them. We also show that the directly fitted slope of the temperature-redshift relation is compatible with (but slightly smaller than) the one inferred from FIRAS, and that standard cosmography lore, based on scale factor expansions, does not apply to this observable, e.g. Padé approximants have no meaningful advantage over plain Taylor series.

AI.tldr: This paper uses cosmography (a model-independent approach) and astrophysical measurements (Sunyaev-Zeldovich + high-resolution spectroscopy, z=0-6.34) to constrain violations of the standard T(z)=T₀(1+z) relation. Violations are constrained to percent level with a single non-standard parameter. Different expansion choices have some impact; Padé approximants show no advantage over Taylor series for this observable.
AI.motivation: The temperature-redshift relation T(z)=T₀(1+z) is fundamental to the standard cosmological model but is violated in many extensions (e.g., photon non-conservation). The authors aim to test these violations model-independently using cosmography.
AI.method: Apply cosmography (model-independent Taylor/Padé expansions) to the T(z) observable. Use Sunyaev-Zeldovich and high-resolution spectroscopy data across 0≤z≤6.34. Compare different expansion variables and approaches, and compare cosmographic constraints with the canonical adiabatic Lima extension model.
AI.result: Violations constrained to percent level; a single non-standard parameter suffices. The fitted slope is compatible with (slightly smaller than) FIRAS-inferred values. Standard cosmography lore does not apply — Padé approximants have no meaningful advantage over Taylor series for this observable.
AI.conclusion: The standard T(z) relation holds to percent level; model-independent cosmography works but standard expansion preferences (e.g., Padé) do not hold for this observable.

title: Neighbors, Not Kin: Kinematic evidence for tidal tails from NGC 7492 along the Sagittarius stream
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. Abstract
summary: The formation, extension, and morphology of extra-tidal stars around globular clusters depend on the internal kinematics of the host cluster and the Galactic potential. Tracing the kinematics of faint tidal tails sheds light on their formation and contribution to the Milky Way halo. NGC 7492 is an outer halo globular cluster with conflicting evidence regarding the presence of tidal tails. If present, the tails are expected to be faint and overlap on the sky with the Sagittarius stream, located at a similar heliocentric distance but with distinct kinematics. We carried out a GIRAFFE spectroscopic follow-up of ten fields covering the expected tidal tails of NGC 7492. Gaia parallaxes were used to remove foreground contaminants, while only loose proper-motion constraints were applied in the target selection. Radial velocities and metallicities were derived for more than 700 stars, from the red giant branch to the upper main sequence. Cluster and extra-tidal stars were identified from their proper motions, radial velocities, and metallicities. This population extends at least 1.8 deg from the cluster center, confirming the tidal tails previously detected only photometrically, with positions consistent with particle-spray models of the cluster disruption. The Sagittarius stream is clearly identified through its distinct proper motions, radial velocities, and more metal-rich population. Despite the low spatial density of the extra-tidal stars, their kinematic signature is clearly detected, demonstrating that the tidal tails overlap on the sky with the Sagittarius stream but are physically unrelated. This spectroscopic dataset provides a robust basis for future studies of the tails at larger angular extents and fainter magnitudes.
